This number almost broke YouTube. 🤯

In 2014 one K-pop video hit 2,147,483,647 views, the biggest number its 32-bit view counter could hold. One more view and it would have flipped to −2,147,483,648. Engineers saw it coming and moved to 64 bits (limit: ~9.2 quintillion). Then they hid an easter egg that spun the counter negative anyway.

One update. 8.5 million computers. Dead. 💀

On 19 July 2024, a faulty CrowdStrike file went to every machine at once (Microsoft estimates ~8.5M Windows PCs crashed). Flights grounded, hospital appointments postponed, TV off air. Pulled after 78 minutes, but millions had to be fixed by hand.

The rule: staged rollouts. Ship to 1% first, so if it breaks, only 1% breaks.

7 crore people. One cricket ball. The same second. 🏏

The T20 World Cup final (8 March 2026) hit 7+ crore concurrent viewers on JioHotstar, a live-streaming world record (ICC figure). How it held: servers switched on BEFORE the match, video chopped into tiny chunks served from nearby servers, and 'panic mode' that turns off extras to keep the match playing.

Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp. Gone for ~6 hours. 📵

On 4 Oct 2021, a routine maintenance command cut Facebook's data centers off its backbone. Its DNS servers, built to go quiet when they can't reach the data centers, withdrew themselves from the internet, so no one could even find facebook.com. The tools to fix it depended on the same network, so engineers had to go on site.

One customer changed one setting. Huge parts of the internet went down. 🌐💥

On 8 June 2021, Amazon, Reddit, the New York Times and gov.uk all showed errors. They shared one CDN: Fastly. A bug shipped in May lay dormant until a customer pushed a perfectly valid config change, and 85% of Fastly's network returned errors. Spotted in 1 minute, 95% back in 49.

A tenth of a second. That's all it takes. ⏱️💸

Around 2006, Amazon engineers slowed pages on purpose and found every extra 100 ms cost about 1% of sales (Greg Linden). Google saw half a second slower → 20% fewer searches (Marissa Mayer). That's why Google now grades every site on Core Web Vitals: loading (LCP), responsiveness (INP), visual stability (CLS).

23 seconds before you could tap anything. 🥶

Pinterest's old mobile site (average Android, slow 3G) took 23 s to become interactive: over 2.5 MB of JavaScript to parse first. The 2017 rebuild split the code and shipped only what each page needed: core JS ~620 KB → 150 KB, time to interactive 23 s → 5.6 s. Time spent +40%, user-generated ad revenue +44%.

Netflix removed React from its landing page… and got 50% faster. 🍿

In 2017 Netflix kept React on the server to build the logged-out homepage, but swapped client-side React (and libraries like Lodash) for plain JavaScript. ~200 KB less JS, time-to-interactive cut by over 50%. Then it prefetched React for the next sign-up steps while you read.

You tap a link. The page jumps. You hit an ad. 😤

Yahoo! JAPAN News (22B+ page views a month) found its article pages jumping as late images pushed text down. The fix: reserve each image's space before it loads. Layout shift went from ~0.2 to ~0, and pages per session rose 15%, sessions got 13% longer (web.dev case study).

Your Hinge match was picked by a Nobel Prize–winning algorithm. 💘

Hinge's Most Compatible uses a version of the Gale–Shapley algorithm (1962, the 'stable marriage problem'; Shapley shared the 2012 Nobel in economics) plus machine learning. Everyone ranks, one side proposes, better offers win, repeat until nobody wants to switch. Hinge says in tests people were 8x more likely to go on a date with their Most Compatible.

On Bumble, an AI looks at some photos before you do. 🛡️

Private Detector (launched 2019) scans images sent in chat; if one looks explicit it arrives blurred, with a warning, and you choose to view, block or report. It was reported as 98% accurate in testing. Only ~0.1% of users send these, but Bumble's scale gave it a huge training set. In 2022 Bumble open-sourced it on GitHub (Apache-2.0).
